subject: Biology
title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
summary: Breathing (ventilation) draws in atmospheric air and releases CO₂-rich air. Respiration then includes gas exchange in the alveoli, transport of gases by blood, exchange at the tissues and use of O₂ by cells.
Inspiration is active — contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases thoracic volume, pressure drops below atmospheric and air flows in. Normal expiration is passive.
Gas exchange is by simple diffusion and depends on the partial pressure gradient, solubility and membrane thickness. CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble than O₂.

About 97% of O₂ travels bound to haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin) and 3% dissolved in plasma. Of CO₂, 20–25% goes as carbamino-haemoglobin, ~70% as bicarbonate and ~7% dissolved in plasma. The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the rhythm of breathing.

formulas.name: Respiratory volumes
formulas.mistake: RV can never be breathed out — so a spirometer cannot measure RV or TLC directly.

formulas.name: Inspiratory capacity
formulas.when: Air that can be inhaled after a normal expiration.

formulas.name: Expiratory capacity
formulas.when: Air that can be exhaled after a normal inspiration.

formulas.name: Functional residual capacity
formulas.when: Air left in the lungs after a normal expiration.

formulas.name: Vital capacity
formulas.when: Maximum air breathed out after a forced inspiration.

formulas.name: Total lung capacity
formulas.formula: TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = VC + RV
formulas.when: Total air in the lungs after a forced inspiration.

formulas.name: Pulmonary ventilation
formulas.formula: minute volume = TV × breathing rate ≈ 500 × 12–16 = 6000–8000 mL/min
formulas.note: A healthy adult breathes 12–16 times a minute.

formulas.name: Partial pressures (mm Hg)
formulas.formula: pO₂ / pCO₂:  atmosphere 159 / 0.3;  alveoli 104 / 40;  deoxygenated blood 40 / 45;  oxygenated blood 95 / 40;  tissues 40 / 45
formulas.note: A gas always moves from higher to lower partial pressure.

formulas.name: Diffusion membrane
formulas.formula: alveolar squamous epithelium + basement substance + capillary endothelium (total < 1 mm)

formulas.name: Oxygen transport
formulas.formula: 97% by Hb (oxyhaemoglobin, each Hb up to 4 O₂);  3% in plasma;  100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers ~5 mL O₂ to tissues

formulas.name: Oxygen dissociation curve
formulas.formula: % saturation vs pO₂ — sigmoid curve;  in alveoli high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺, low T ⇒ oxyhaemoglobin forms;  in tissues the reverse ⇒ O₂ is released
formulas.when: When Hb takes up or releases O₂.
formulas.note: A right shift (Bohr effect) means O₂ is released more easily.

formulas.name: CO₂ transport
formulas.formula: 20–25% carbamino-haemoglobin;  ~70% bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻);  ~7% dissolved in plasma;  100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers ~4 mL CO₂ to the alveoli

formulas.name: Carbonic anhydrase reaction
formulas.formula: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺   (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs, a little in plasma)
formulas.note: The reaction goes forward in tissues and backward in the alveoli.

formulas.name: Regulation of respiration
formulas.formula: respiratory rhythm centre (medulla);  pneumotaxic centre (pons) — shortens inspiration and so raises the rate;  chemosensitive area (medulla) — sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺;  receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery
formulas.note: O₂ plays only a small role in the rhythm; CO₂/H⁺ are the main signals.

examples.title: O₂ delivery
examples.problem: Cardiac output is 5 L/min and each 100 mL of blood delivers ~5 mL O₂. O₂ delivered to tissues per minute?

examples.title: Direction of diffusion
examples.problem: Between alveoli (pO₂ 104, pCO₂ 40) and deoxygenated blood (pO₂ 40, pCO₂ 45), which way do the gases move?
examples.solution: O₂ moves from alveoli to blood (104 → 40), CO₂ from blood to alveoli (45 → 40). The CO₂ gradient is small, but its 20–25 times higher solubility lets plenty of CO₂ diffuse.

examples.title: Emphysema
examples.problem: Why is breathing difficult in emphysema?
examples.solution: Alveolar walls are damaged and the respiratory surface decreases — cigarette smoking is the main cause.

topics.title: Respiratory organs in animals
topics.explain: Lower invertebrates (sponges, coelenterates, flatworms) — simple diffusion over the body surface. Earthworm — moist cuticle. Insects — tracheal tubes. Aquatic arthropods and molluscs — gills (branchial respiration). Fish — gills. Amphibians — skin (cutaneous) and lungs. Reptiles, birds, mammals — lungs (pulmonary respiration).

topics.title: Human respiratory system
topics.explain: External nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx (sound box; the epiglottis stops food entering) → trachea → primary, secondary, tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea to the initial bronchioles. Lungs are covered by double-layered pleura; pleural fluid reduces friction. The conducting part filters, warms and moistens air; the exchange part is the alveoli.

topics.title: Mechanism of breathing
topics.explain: Inspiration: the diaphragm contracts (moves down) and external intercostal muscles contract (lifting ribs and sternum) ⇒ thoracic and pulmonary volume increase ⇒ intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric ⇒ air flows in. Expiration: muscles relax ⇒ volume falls ⇒ pressure rises ⇒ air flows out. Abdominal muscles help in forced breathing.

topics.title: Exchange of gases
topics.explain: Alveoli are the primary site, tissues the secondary site. Diffusion depends on the partial pressure gradient, gas solubility and membrane thickness. The diffusion membrane is very thin (< 1 mm).

topics.title: Transport of gases
topics.explain: Haemoglobin (the red iron pigment of RBCs) binds O₂ reversibly. At high pCO₂, CO₂ binds Hb as carbamino-haemoglobin and is released in the alveoli. Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs forms bicarbonate.

topics.title: Disorders of respiratory system
topics.explain: Asthma: inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles causes wheezing and difficulty in breathing. Emphysema: a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged and respiratory surface decreases — mainly caused by smoking. Occupational respiratory disorders: dust (stone breaking, grinding) causes fibrosis of the lungs — protective masks should be worn.

ratta: IC = TV + IRV;  EC = TV + ERV;  FRC = ERV + RV;  VC = ERV + TV + IRV;  TLC = VC + RV.
Alveoli pO₂ 104, pCO₂ 40;  tissues pO₂ 40, pCO₂ 45.
O₂: 97% Hb, 3% plasma;  100 mL blood → 5 mL O₂.
CO₂: 20–25% carbamino, 70% HCO₃⁻, 7% plasma;  4 mL per 100 mL.
Rhythm centre in medulla;  pneumotaxic centre in pons.
Emphysema — smoking;  asthma — inflammation of bronchi.
